newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Taxes may push Ericsson out of Sweden.
newsitem.headline: Taxes may push Ericsson out of Sweden.

text.p: Swedish mobile phone giant Ericsson joined a growing chorus of companies who say a poor business climate and crushing taxation in Sweden may force them to move operations overseas.
In a radio interview at the weekend, Ericsson's chief executive Lars Ramqvist said the company board had decided to look into a possible move of the Stockholm head office.
The Swedish crown weakened on Monday and some traders said Ramqvist's comments were partly responsible.

"The investigation should be seen in the light that only three percent of our business is in Sweden," Ramqvist told the radio. "In addition, the owners would like to see how we can recruit managers to Ericsson in the long-term," Ramqvist said.

Ericsson has said it was dissatisfied with the government's plan to phase out Sweden's nuclear programme, high marginal taxes which scare away well-educated workers and laws preventing companies from buying back their own shares.
"For tax reasons it is almost hopeless to get a foreigner to move here," Ramqvist told the radio. Highly paid employees routinely pay 60 percent of their salaries in tax.
"If politicians don't understand that we must reward development and competence, Ericsson won't manage the restructuring we are facing," Ramqvist said.
"If our development people would rather move to the U.S. or Britain, what will we do then?"
Ericsson has some 94,000 employees in 130 countries. Some 43,000 employees are in Sweden. Of these, about 20,000 are in the Stockholm area and the rest in some 20 other Swedish cities.
Its net sales in 1996 totalled 124.27 billion crowns ($15.8 billion) and it posted a profit of 10.15 billion crowns before tax in that year.

News of the report, which is due to be ready before the summer, prompted comments by Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros, who said the government was looking into new tax rules for key foreign staffers.
"If they only stay a few years they don't have the same need for the services our taxes are financing," he was quoted by daily Dagens Nyheter as saying.
Critics hinted that the government needed to take more drastic measures.
"This is devastating for the possbilities of making Sweden again a successful industrial nation which is competitive in high technology," said Lars Leijonborg, head of Sweden's Liberal Party.
"Ericsson's plans to move are a sign of the country's poor business climate," said Lars Tobisson, of the conservative Moderate party.
"Personal taxation laws make it difficult for Ericsson and other large companies to retain qualified key personel in Sweden," he added.
Neighboring Finland and other European countries have special tax rules for foreigners.

A foreign boss who earns more than 35,000 Finnish markka a month pays a maximum of 35 percent in tax, while the corresponding tax rate for a Finnish boss with the same salary is 70 percent, daily Dagens Nyheter said.
Industry and Commerce Minister Anders Sundstrom defended the Swedish business climate, saying that it had contributed to Ericsson's success.
"Ericsson has had fantastic development and this development perhaps does not just depend on Ramqvist and serveral others, but on the environment which the company has worked in," Sundstrom said.
At home Ramqvist has had to defend Ericsson's decision to outsource the manufacture of circuit boards in a restructuring move that affected 1,400 employees in the town of Norrkoping.
"Everything depends on what the competition does. One year ago I did not know we would be forced to make cut-backs...," Ramqvist said.
"Competition from U.S. printed circuit board manufacturers, who make the cards more cheaply than we do, did not exist then," Ramqvist said. ($ = 7.878 Swedish Crowns)
